name: ps
description: Reports a snapshot of current processes. The classic Unix style (ps aux) and BSD style are the most common.

flags.description: BSD style: all processes (a), including those without a terminal (x), with owner, CPU%, MEM%, and command (u).
System V style: all processes with full formatting, parent PIDs.
Show the process tree with ASCII-art parent-child relationships.
Sort by memory usage descending (also -%cpu, pid).
-C NAME: only the given PID / command name.

examples.output:
USER  PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY  STAT START TIME COMMAND
root    1  0.0  0.2 167312 11876 ?   Ss   08:00 0:02 /sbin/init
user  2140  0.5  1.1 482916 45220 pts/0 Ss 09:00 0:01 -bash
examples.explanation: Every running process. Key columns: PID (process ID), %CPU/%MEM (resource use), STAT (S=sleeping, R=running, Z=zombie), COMMAND.
Shows the process hierarchy — which process spawned which. Init/systemd (PID 1) is the root of the tree.

examples.output:
USER  PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY  STAT START TIME COMMAND
mysql 1187  1.2 18.3 1984212 1500000 ? Sl 08:00 3:12 /usr/sbin/mysqld
examples.explanation: The five biggest memory consumers — the first step when a server is running out of RAM.
All processes owned by alice, useful before terminating a user's session.

about: ps shows a SNAPSHOT — for continuously updating views use top or htop. STAT codes worth knowing: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible sleep (usually I/O), Z zombie, T stopped, < high priority, N low priority, s session leader, + foreground.
useCases: Find a process ID to kill or inspect.
See the process tree to understand service relationships.
mistakes: Typing ps -aux — mixing styles; use ps aux or ps -ef.
Expecting live updates from ps — it is a snapshot; use top.
